person.name: Mercy_Otis_Warren
person.summary: Mercy Otis Warren was a Massachusetts playwright, poet, pamphleteer, and political writer during the American Revolution. Her satires challenged royal rule, and her three-volume history recorded the Revolution from the Stamp Act through the formation of the United States.

conclusion: Mercy Otis Warren used anonymous plays and pamphlets to oppose royal authority in Massachusetts. In 1788 she argued for a Bill of Rights during the ratification debate. Her three-volume History of the Rise, Progress, and Termination of the American Revolution appeared in 1805.

events.title: Birth in Barnstable
events.description: Mercy Otis was born into the Barnstable household of James Otis and Mary Allyne Otis. James Otis farmed and practiced law. He opposed British rule, and the Otis children grew up amid revolutionary ideals.

events.title: Studies with Her Brothers
events.description: Reverend Jonathan Russell tutored Mercy Otis's brothers Joseph and James for college in Barnstable. Mercy studied with them. Her father, James Otis, supported her reading and writing.

events.title: Marries James Warren
events.description: Mercy Otis married her second cousin James Warren in Barnstable on November 14, 1754. James Warren worked as a merchant and farmer. The couple made their home in Plymouth.
events.background:
The marriage concluded a six-year engagement. James Warren had returned to Plymouth after graduating from Harvard College in 1745. He built his livelihood there as a merchant and gentleman farmer. The ceremony was held at the Otis family residence.

Their Plymouth household began in a homestead James Warren bought in 1755. When his father died two years later, James succeeded him as high sheriff of Plymouth County. The couple then moved to the Warren family estate.

events.title: Organizes Patriot Meetings
events.description: Mercy Otis Warren hosted Patriot meetings at her Plymouth home as resistance to British rule intensified. She worked with James Warren, Samuel Adams, Joseph Warren, and other Patriots. Their meetings helped establish [[committee of correspondence|committees of correspondence]], town bodies that shared political information and organized resistance.

committee of correspondence.explanation: These committees connected towns and colonies during the imperial crisis. They circulated news, coordinated action, and helped turn local protest into intercolonial resistance.

events.title: Publishes The Adulateur
events.description: Mercy Otis Warren published The Adulateur, an anonymous satirical play, in 1773. The drama attacked Thomas Hutchinson through the character Rapatio. Its character Brutus represented her brother James Otis Jr. and the Patriot cause.

event_class.title: The Adulateur
event_class.impact: The play was well received in Massachusetts, where Thomas Hutchinson's political opponents called him Rapatio.

events.background:
The 1773 publication appeared within a longer play by an unknown author. Warren had not consented to its inclusion. Her Whig politics shaped the play’s treatment of its opposing factions. Whig characters are brave and independent. Tory characters are selfish and rude. The story ends with a victory for the Whig side.

Its success encouraged Warren to continue using drama for political commentary.

events.title: Publishes The Group
events.description: As fighting began between Britain and the colonies, Mercy Otis Warren anonymously published The Group in 1775. The satire imagines a king cancelling the [[Massachusetts charter|charter that governed colonial Massachusetts]]. It attacks officials who supported royal authority.

Massachusetts charter.explanation: A colonial charter set the legal basis for Massachusetts's government. Conflict over colonial rights under royal rule was central to the imperial crisis.

events.title: Publishes The Blockheads
events.description: Mercy Otis Warren anonymously published The Blockheads, a satirical play, in 1776. The play criticized British authority during the Revolutionary War.

events.title: Opposes Constitution Ratification
events.description: Mercy Otis Warren published Observations on the New Constitution, and on the Federal and State Conventions in 1788 under the name A Columbian Patriot. She opposed ratification of the proposed Constitution. She called for a [[Bill of Rights]] to protect individual liberties.

Bill of Rights.explanation: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments to the United States Constitution. It lists protections for individual liberties and limits on government power.

events.background: The pamphlet circulated without a secure public attribution for many years. Elbridge Gerry was among the writers thought to have produced it. A reference in Warren’s 1787 letter to the British historian Catharine Macaulay later provided the evidence that credited Warren with its authorship. Her descendant Charles Warren found the letter.

events.title: Claims Her Name
events.description: Mercy Otis Warren published Poems, Dramatic and Miscellaneous under her own name in Boston in 1790. The collection brought together political poems and plays about liberty, civic conduct, and the new republic.

events.title: Gathers Revolutionary Records
events.description: Mercy Otis Warren asked George Washington to approve her proposed history of the American Revolution in 1790. She drew on her memory of the conflict. She also collected congressional debates, letters, and accounts from participants.

events.title: Publishes Revolutionary History
events.description: Mercy Otis Warren published History of the Rise, Progress, and Termination of the American Revolution in 1805. Health problems, periods of blindness, and the deaths of three sons delayed its completion. Thomas Jefferson ordered copies for himself and his cabinet. John Adams objected to Warren's account of his part in the Revolution.

images.caption: Title page of Warren’s Revolutionary history
images.creator: Mercy Otis Warren (1728–1814)

event_class.title: History of the Rise, Progress, and Termination of the American Revolution
event_class.impact: Thomas Jefferson ordered copies of the history for himself and members of his cabinet.

events.background:
Warren had begun drafting the history while the Revolution was still underway. She added to those drafts for four years before the book appeared. Its 1,317 pages followed events from the Stamp Act through the writing and ratification of the Constitution. Roughly one-third of the narrative concerned the period after Yorktown.

The book used a personal style and referred to its author in the third person. It also advanced contested judgments about the Revolution. Warren treated the Battle of Yorktown as something other than a true battle. Adams called her account a radical simplification and sometimes a falsification of the Revolution's history. Their letters after publication argued fiercely over his role.

In 1815, Jefferson sold books from his collection to the Library of Congress. A fire on Christmas Eve 1851 destroyed almost two-thirds of that collection. The history nearly burned with it, and its title page was singed.

events.title: Reconciles with John Adams
events.description: Mercy Otis Warren reconciled with John Adams in 1812. Adams had objected to her account of his role in [[History of the Rise, Progress, and Termination of the American Revolution]].

events.title: Death in Plymouth
events.description: Mercy Otis Warren died in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on October 19, 1814, at age 86. She had survived her husband, James Warren, by six years.
